subtopics.title: Origin and Objective
subtopics.summary: The Anti-Defection Law was introduced through the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985, and placed in the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution. Its objective is to prevent political defections and ensure stability in governments. The phrase 'Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' is linked to frequent party-switching by legislators in the 1960s. The law applies to both Parliament and State Assemblies.
facts: Introduced through the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985
Enshrined in the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution
Objective: prevent political defections and ensure stability in governments
Phrase 'Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' linked to frequent party-switching in the 1960s
Applies to both Parliament and State Legislatures
Constitutional basis: Articles 102(1) and 191(1)
Lays down the process for disqualifying legislators on grounds of defection

subtopics.title: Grounds for Disqualification
subtopics.summary: A legislator loses membership if they voluntarily give up party membership or vote or abstain contrary to the party whip. Under Articles 102(1) and 191(1), a legislator can also be disqualified for holding an office of profit, being declared of unsound mind by a court, being an undischarged insolvent, losing Indian citizenship or showing allegiance to another country, or being disqualified under any law made by Parliament. The booklet also lists joining another party and opposing party direction as grounds in the disqualification summary.
facts: Voluntarily giving up party membership is a ground for disqualification
Voting or abstaining contrary to the party whip is a ground for disqualification
Holding an office of profit is a ground under Articles 102(1) and 191(1)
Being declared of unsound mind by a court is a ground
Being an undischarged insolvent is a ground
Losing Indian citizenship or showing allegiance to another country is a ground
Disqualification under any law made by Parliament is a ground

subtopics.title: Exceptions, Mergers and Member Categories
subtopics.summary: A party can merge without disqualification if two-thirds of the members of a legislature party agree, a provision retained after the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003. That amendment removed the earlier split provision, under which one-third of members could split without disqualification. A whip breach is excused if prior permission is taken or the party condones the action within 15 days. Independent members are disqualified for joining a party after election, while nominated members are disqualified for joining after six months of nomination.
facts: Merger: no disqualification if two-thirds of a legislature party agree to merge
Earlier, one-third of members could split without disqualification
The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act (2003) removed the split provision
Whip exception: prior permission taken, or party condones the action within 15 days
Independent member: disqualified if they join a party after election
Nominated member: disqualified if they join a party after six months of nomination
Merger provision is an exception to disqualification under the law

subtopics.title: Deciding Authority and Judicial Review
subtopics.summary: The Speaker (Lok Sabha) or the Chairman (Rajya Sabha) decides disqualification petitions, and the decision is subject to judicial review. Keisham Meghachandra Singh vs Speaker Manipur (2020) says such decisions should ideally be made within 3 months. The grounds for reviewing a Speaker's decision, laid down in Shrimanth Balasaheb Patil vs Speaker Karnataka (2019), include violation of a constitutional mandate, malafide intent, a perverse decision, and failure to follow natural justice.
facts: Speaker (Lok Sabha) or Chairman (Rajya Sabha) decides disqualification
Decision of the Speaker or Chairman is subject to judicial review
Kihoto Hollohan vs Zachillhu (1992): Speaker's decisions subject to judicial review
Keisham Meghachandra Singh vs Speaker Manipur (2020): decisions ideally within 3 months
Shrimanth Balasaheb Patil vs Speaker Karnataka (2019): review grounds include malafide intent and perverse decision
Ravi S Naik vs Union of India: membership can be inferred from members' conduct

subtopics.title: Significance, Criticisms and Key Issues
subtopics.summary: The law allows party mergers without disqualifying members, prevents defections for office or material gain, and supports party stability and discipline. Critics point to long delays in deciding disqualification petitions, allegations that presiding officers act partisanly, and limited judicial intervention before the Speaker decides. They also argue that the two-thirds merger clause enables mass defections and that the rigid whip system reduces intra-party democracy.
facts: Prevents defections for office or material gain
Ensures party stability and prevents government instability
Ensures party discipline through adherence to the whip
Makes legislators accountable for their conduct
Key issue: disqualification petitions often remain pending for long durations
Key issue: allegations of bias, as Speaker or Chairman may act partisanly
Key issue: courts typically intervene only after the Speaker's decision
Key issue: rigid whip system, including whips on non-critical matters
Key issue: two-thirds merger clause enables large-scale defections

quizzes.passage: Changing parties after being elected has long been a concern in Indian politics. An old expression, often quoted in this context, describes members who switched their political loyalties again and again, and it is linked to a period of frequent shifts among legislators. The rules that address this problem form part of the Constitution. They sit in a dedicated schedule, which groups the provisions on the subject together. These rules were brought in through a constitutional amendment, so they were added to the Constitution rather than passed as an ordinary statute. Two officers play a central role when a complaint is raised under them: the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. Their decisions matter because they determine whether a member keeps a seat. The booklet also records that these decisions have been the subject of concern for some time. The subject has also been examined in several Supreme Court judgments, which the booklet lists in its discussion of the topic. Those judgments deal with the powers of presiding officers and the extent to which courts may review their decisions. Taken together, the origin of the rules, their place in the Constitution, and the officers who apply them form the basic background for understanding how the framework works in practice.

quizzes.passage: A legislator does not lose membership simply because he or she disagrees with a colleague or a party leader. The rules on loss of membership are set out as a list of specific grounds, and the list covers both a member's conduct and his or her personal circumstances. Some grounds relate to choices a member makes in connection with a political party. Others relate to the member's status and to certain personal circumstances. Decisions on these grounds are made by the presiding officer of the house. A ground must be clearly made out before a seat can be lost, and the rules do not treat every political disagreement as a reason to remove a member. The grounds are set out in the Constitution and in the law itself, so the presiding officer applies a fixed checklist rather than an open-ended power. Membership of a legislature therefore depends on whether one of the listed grounds applies, and the booklet describes the grounds in some detail for this reason. When a listed ground is found to apply, the member can lose the seat. The booklet sets out these grounds one after another, so that each can be checked separately against the facts of a particular case. Each ground is a distinct condition, and a member is judged against the specific ground that has been alleged.

quizzes.passage: A legislator can lose a seat only on grounds set out in a fixed list, not because of ordinary political disagreement. The list covers a member's conduct and personal circumstances. Some grounds concern choices a member makes in relation to a political party, such as conduct in the House. Other grounds concern the member's standing and legal position. Decisions on disqualification are taken by the presiding officer of the house, namely the Speaker of the Lok Sabha or the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The presiding officer must establish that a ground applies before a seat is lost. The grounds are set out in the Constitution and in the law itself, so the presiding officer applies a fixed checklist rather than an open-ended power. Courts can review such decisions in certain circumstances, which is one reason the topic attracts attention. The booklet presents these grounds as a framework that governs when a member's place in the House is at risk. Each ground is a separate condition, and the presiding officer looks at the specific ground that has been alleged. The booklet sets out the grounds one after another, which makes it possible to check each one on its own terms. A member who is not caught by any listed ground keeps the seat, whatever the political disagreement may be.

quizzes.passage: Rules that govern elected members are often discussed in terms of their purpose and their effect on everyday politics. The booklet describes the framework as one that serves several functions, and it also records the concerns that critics have raised. The framework gives certain officers the job of deciding complaints, and those officers hold their posts within the legislature. Courts have a limited role, since they generally examine a matter only after the relevant officer has ruled on it. Party leaders issue instructions to members, and the booklet describes these instructions as applying in a wide range of situations. The merger provision is another point of discussion, since it allows members to act together in certain circumstances. The booklet also raises the question of how long complaints take to be resolved, which adds to the wider debate. Together these points give the reader a fuller view of how the framework works and why it attracts attention. The rules sit within the Constitution, which gives them a place among its provisions on the conduct of legislators. The booklet sets out the purposes of the framework, the officers who apply it, and the points on which it has drawn criticism, and these are discussed in turn. Several of the points are closely connected, so the reader is best served by seeing how they fit together.
